title: Footings, post setting and levels
audience: Deck and fence workers who set footings and posts and are paid for the higher-rate structural work
learningOutcomes: Describe the footing and post-setting checks that must be done before a deck or fence is loaded.
Set posts and levels to the approved design, and record the check.
Identify when footing and structural work is licensed or needs a permit, and refer it.

instruction.heading: Footings carry the structure
instruction.body: A footing transfers the load of a deck or fence into the ground. Its size, depth, and the concrete or fixing method come from the approved design, the ground conditions and the load. They are not chosen on site from habit or convenience. Before any excavation, confirm that the design is approved for the job, that the permit position has been checked under “Deck and fence scope, permits and boundary survey”, and that the footing details on site match the approved drawing. Where the ground is different from the design assumes, such as rock, soft fill or a slope, stop and refer the change. Do not change the depth or the size on site to suit the conditions. Concrete footings and timber or metal posts are the parts of a deck or fence that most often fail when they are set wrongly, and they are also the parts that are hardest to correct once the work is finished.

instruction.heading: Services and excavation
instruction.body: Check for underground services before digging. The Before You Dig Australia guidance says that anyone working near underground assets must understand their duty of care, and that plans show that infrastructure is present but not its exact position. The guidance describes lodging a plan request at least one day before the work begins, and checking that every asset owner has responded before work starts. Look for surface clues such as meters, marker posts, inspection points and warning signs. Use a skilled locator where one is available. Where a cable or pipe is found, the guidance describes exposing it by hand where that is safe and appropriate. Stop and refer if services are found where the design did not show them.

instruction.heading: Set posts and check levels
instruction.body: Set each post plumb and at the design height, and check the level across the structure before the concrete cures. Brace each post so it cannot move while the concrete sets, and check the brace again after the first pour. A post that looks plumb at ground level can be well out of line at the top of a long deck or fence, so take readings at the height the design names, not only at the base. Record the readings for each post, and photograph the set posts before backfilling. Where a reading falls outside the tolerance in the design, do not force the post into line. Reset the post, or refer the change. Forcing a post after the concrete has begun to set can crack the footing and loosen the post.

instruction.heading: Concrete cure and loading
instruction.body: Do not load a post, a rail or a deck frame until the concrete has cured for the period the supplier and the design state. The cure period depends on the mix, the weather and the placement, so use the supplier's stated period for the product, and record the time the concrete was placed and the time it may be loaded. Keep the record of the cure time with the footing record, and do not load a post early to meet a programme date.

instruction.heading: Licence positions by state
instruction.body: The licence question for footing and structural work depends on the state and on the exact wording of the licence page. In New South Wales, the carpentry page names timber decks and timber and metal fencing, but only under concreting for footings or structural support. A contractor licence is needed for building or trade work valued at more than $5,000 in labour and materials, including GST. The fencing page applies the same $5,000 threshold to fencing work regardless of materials. In Queensland, the QBCC licence page sets a $3,300 threshold for building work, and does not name fences or decks. The QBCC fence guide says a fence on non-agricultural land valued under $3,300 does not need a licence, and it does not say whether labour and GST count. In Victoria, the Consumer Affairs Victoria page says domestic building work with a contract over $10,000 needs registration, and it does not mention decks. Confirm the position for the state and the job before pricing.

procedure: Confirm the approved design, the permit position and the footing size and depth on the drawing.
Request the service plans and check that every asset owner has responded. Locate services by surface clues and the locator, and stop if services are found where none were shown.
Excavate to the design depth, check the base against the design, and do not reduce the depth on site.
Set each post plumb and at the design height, and brace it before the concrete sets.
Check the levels across the structure, and record the plumb and level readings for each post.
Photograph the set posts before backfilling, and record the placement and cure times.
Do not load the post, rail or frame until the cure time has passed, and record when it was loaded.

workedExamples.situation: A client asks for a fence footing to be dug 200 millimetres shallower than the design, to save time on rock. This example is for training.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the footing be dug shallower?
workedExamples.reasoning: No. The footing depth comes from the approved design and the ground conditions. Rock is a reason to refer the design change to the designer or the approving authority, not a reason to reduce the depth on site. Record the request and the referral, and price any change as a separate variation. The 200 millimetre figure is an example, not a standard.

workedExamples.situation: A post begins to lean after the concrete is placed, because the bracing was knocked. This is an example job.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you do before the concrete sets?
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop the work on that post, and check the brace and the post position against the design. Reset the post if the design tolerance is still possible, and re-brace it. Do not force the post back while the concrete is setting, because this can crack the footing. If the reading still falls outside the design tolerance, refer the change. Record the readings before and after, and the action taken.

workedExamples.situation: Before digging a fence footing, a worker finds a marker post and a metal cover that the plan did not show. This is an example job.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop digging near the marker and cover. Do not dig to see what is underneath. Check the plan with the asset owner, use a skilled locator where available, and expose any cable or pipe only by the method the guidance allows. Refer any change to the footing location, and record the findings before work resumes.

equipmentAndPpe: Approved design drawing with footing size, depth, post height and tolerance
Spirit level, string line and plumb bob, with a record sheet for readings
Post braces and stakes, checked before each pour
Excavation tools, with a service locator where available and the plan on site
Eye protection and gloves for concrete work, and closed footwear

commonErrors.error: Reducing the footing depth on site to save time.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the approved design depth, and refer any change in writing before the work continues.

commonErrors.error: Loading a post before the concrete has cured.
commonErrors.prevention: Record the placement and cure times, and do not load the post until the stated time has passed.

commonErrors.error: Excavating without checking for underground services.
commonErrors.prevention: Request the plan, confirm responses from asset owners, and stop if services are found.

commonErrors.error: Removing the brace before the concrete has set.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep the brace in place until the concrete has set, and check it after the first pour.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a $5,000 threshold means no licence is needed below that value in every state.
commonErrors.prevention: Check each state's licence page and its wording, because the thresholds and the work covered differ.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: New South Wales: the carpentry page names timber decks and timber and metal fencing under concreting for footings or structural support, with a contractor licence needed above $5,000 in labour and materials including GST. The fencing page sets the same threshold for fencing work.
Queensland: the QBCC licence page sets a $3,300 threshold for building work. The QBCC fence guide sets the same figure for fences on non-agricultural land.
Victoria: domestic building work with a contract over $10,000 needs registration, and the page does not mention decks or fences.
Underground services: check the plan and duty-of-care information before excavation.
Completing this lesson does not give a carpentry, concreting or building licence, or authority to set structural footings or to change a design.

qualityStandard: Footing size and depth match the approved design, and no change is made on site without a written referral.
Posts are plumb, at the design height, and braced until the concrete has set, with the readings recorded.
The service check is done before excavation, and the plan responses are on file.
Loading is held until the recorded cure time has passed.
documentationEvidence: Footing and post-setting record with depths, heights, plumb and level readings
Service plan reference and the record of responses from asset owners
Photographs of the set posts before backfilling, with the date
Record of placement time, cure period and the time the post was loaded
Referral note for any design change, with the reply
summary: Footings and posts follow the approved design, and a change is referred, not made on site.
Check services before excavation, and stop if services are found.
Set posts plumb and at height, brace them, record the readings, and hold loading until the cure time has passed.
Licence thresholds differ by state: New South Wales $5,000 including GST, Queensland $3,300 for building work, and Victoria $10,000 for domestic building work.

knowledgeChecks.question: A client asks for a footing to be dug shallower than the design to save time. What is correct?
options: Dig it shallower to save time on the job and make up the depth with concrete later
Use less concrete instead of changing the depth, since the concrete is the main cost
Dig it shallower, then tell the council afterwards once the footing is in place
Keep the approved depth and refer any change to the designer or approving authority

knowledgeChecks.question: When should a post be loaded?
options: After the concrete has cured for the recorded period
As soon as the post is set, while the mix is still soft
Before the bracing is put in, so the post can settle
Only after the client has inspected it and signed off

knowledgeChecks.question: What must happen before a fence footing is excavated?
options: The neighbour is asked to watch the digging and call out any problems they see along the fence line
The service plan is checked, responses are on file, and the work stops if services are found
A test hole is dug with the machine to see what is there before the plan is checked
No check is needed in a backyard, since services are not usually found in that part of the property
